title: Norwest Corp. v. Commissioner
subject: Internal-Use Software
summary: Norwest Corp. v. Commissioner, 110 T.C. 454 (1998), is a U.S. Tax Court decision setting the standards taxpayers must meet to claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41 for internal-use software. Applying a seven-part test, the Court held that only one of Norwest's eight sample banking software projects, the Strategic Banking System Customer Module, qualified.

body.text: Executive Summary & Case Background

In Norwest Corporation and Subsidiaries v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, 110 T.C. 454 (1998), the United States Tax Court issued a foundational opinion governing the eligibility of internal-use computer software (IUS) for the federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41. Authored by Judge Julian I. Jacobs and filed on June 29, 1998, the ruling adjudicated claims by Norwest Corporation, a Delaware bank holding company headquartered in Minneapolis, Minnesota, whose affiliates provided banking and other financial services (110 T.C. at 458). Between 1986 and 1991, Norwest developed or modified software for the internal management and administration of its businesses, and the parties agreed that $20,552,274 of the $22,658,829 in expenditures claimed for the eight sample software development activities alone had been substantiated (110 T.C. at 454, 457). After the Commissioner had determined income tax deficiencies for 1983 through 1989, Norwest—which had not claimed the research credit on any of its returns for 1986 through 1991—engaged Coopers & Lybrand, LLP, in August 1994 to conduct a retrospective study covering 1986 through 1993; that study concluded that 67 of 118 internal use software development activities qualified, and Norwest amended its Tax Court petitions to claim the credit for 1986 through 1989 and later to carry back credits from 1990 and 1991 to 1989 and increase the credit for 1986 through 1991 (110 T.C. at 456–457 & n.3). To establish a manageable framework for trial, the parties stipulated to a representative sample of eight software development activities conducted between 1986 and 1991, agreeing that the remaining 59 activities would be deemed substantiated in the same 90.7 percent ratio as the sample and would be deemed qualified according to an agreed-upon formula to the extent any of the eight sample activities qualified (110 T.C. at 457).

The Commissioner of Internal Revenue contested Norwest's research credit claims, and the cases were consolidated for trial, briefing, and opinion solely with respect to whether Norwest's activities constituted qualified research under IRC Section 41; the opinion did not adjudicate the computation of the credit base under IRC Section 41(c) (110 T.C. at 454 n.1, 457). The Commissioner's experts asserted that Norwest's software expenditures represented normal and routine software development—installation, interfacing, testing, maintenance, and enhancement of software, including vendor-supplied packages—rather than qualified research aimed at resolving technological uncertainty (110 T.C. at 507–511). Furthermore, the Commissioner contended that because the software was developed for Norwest's internal business purposes, the internal-use software tests should be read narrowly as exceptions to the general exclusion of IRC Section 41(d)(4)(E), requiring the "high threshold of innovation" referenced in the House and Senate reports accompanying the Tax Reform Act of 1986 and in the 1997 proposed regulations (110 T.C. at 498). With respect to project economics and contract research, the Commissioner argued that Norwest did not retain a right to the research results of the work performed by Electronic Data Systems Corp. (EDS) on the Strategic Banking System and that Norwest's payments to EDS were contingent on the success of the research, while his experts characterized the risks Norwest faced as business rather than technical risks (110 T.C. at 513, 518–520). The base-period consistency requirement of IRC Section 41(c) was not raised or decided in the opinion; its implications for credit studies are discussed below as a separate statutory requirement rather than as a holding of Norwest.

Because the Department of the Treasury had not yet promulgated final regulations interpreting the internal-use software exclusion under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(E) when the case was tried—having issued only initial proposed regulations in January 1997 (62 Fed. Reg. 83)—the Tax Court applied the statutory text of IRC Section 41(d) together with the 1986 House Conference Report (H.R. Conf. Rep. No. 99-841, Vol. II), treating the conference report's three internal-use software tests as an expression of legislative intent and applying the resulting seven-part qualification framework that the parties agreed governed the case (110 T.C. at 487–488). Under this framework, a taxpayer claiming Section 41 credits for internal-use software must first satisfy four general statutory tests applicable to all qualified research, followed by three heightened tests specific to internal-use software.

The first general statutory requirement is the Section 174 Expenditure Test under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A), which mandates that research expenditures be eligible for treatment as research or experimental expenses under IRC Section 174; the Court held that this language requires the taxpayer to satisfy all the elements for a deduction under Section 174, including that the expenditures represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2, and it found this test satisfied for all eight sample activities on the basis of the Commissioner's concession (110 T.C. at 489–491). Practitioners evaluating Norwest for current tax planning must account for the statutory evolution of this prong: under Public Law 119-21 (commonly known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted July 4, 2025), Congress introduced IRC Section 174A, which restores immediate domestic research and experimental expensing (or elective capitalization and amortization) for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, and updated Section 41(d)(1)(A) to reference expenditures eligible under Section 174A, while foreign research expenditures remain subject to mandatory 15-year amortization under Section 174. Crucially, as Norwest established, qualification of software development costs under Section 174 or Section 174A is a threshold prerequisite but does not automatically confer eligibility for the Section 41 tax credit.

The second general requirement is the Discovery or Technological Information Test under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(i), which dictates that the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, meaning the activities fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. The third general requirement is the Business Component Test under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), which requires the taxpayer to intend that the discovered technological information be useful in the development of a new or improved business component—defined under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business. The fourth general requirement is the Process of Experimentation Test under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and Section 41(d)(3), which mandates that substantially all of the research activities constitute elements of a structured process of experimentation relating to a qualified purpose—specifically, a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality.

Beyond those four universal statutory tests, Norwest enforced three additional requirements derived from IRC Section 41(d)(4)(E) and the 1986 legislative history that apply specifically to internal-use software. The fifth overall test (and first IUS prong) is the Innovativeness Test, which requires the internal-use software to be innovative, as where the software results in a reduction in cost, or improvement in speed, that is substantial and economically significant—a standard the Court construed as requiring a "high threshold of innovativeness" (110 T.C. at 498–499). The sixth test (second IUS prong) is the Significant Economic Risk Test, under which the software development must entail significant economic risk, as where the taxpayer commits substantial resources to development and there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that those resources would be recovered within a reasonable period (110 T.C. at 499–500). The seventh test (third IUS prong) is the Commercial Availability Test, which requires that the software not be commercially available for purchase, lease, or license by the taxpayer without modifications that independently satisfy the innovativeness and significant economic risk requirements.

Applying this seven-test matrix to the eight representative projects, the Tax Court delivered a decisive split holding that largely favored the Commissioner while preserving a narrow pathway for genuinely pioneering enterprise software architecture. The Court held that only one of the eight representative projects—the Strategic Banking System (SBS) Customer Module—satisfied all seven tests and qualified for the research credit with respect to expenses paid or incurred through the first deployment of the customer module to each of Norwest's banks, while excluding customization activities after receipt of the first SBS release that were unrelated to installation and interfacing, as well as activities performed after the first SBS release was installed at each bank; the SBS deposit and credit modules did not qualify (110 T.C. at 514–515, 520–521). The Court disqualified the remaining seven representative projects (Trust TU, Success, General Ledger, Money Transfer, Cyborg Payroll, Trust Payment, and Debit Card), concluding that they constituted routine software development, vendor package configuration, or standard engineering utilizing known computer science methodologies. Additionally, the Court rejected the Commissioner's contract research challenge to SBS, holding that Norwest had a right to the research results through its perpetual, royalty-free license from EDS and that its payments were not contingent on the success of the research; the opinion contains no finding that Norwest lacked substantial rights in any vendor-related project (110 T.C. at 518–520). Finally, the opinion did not decide any computational issue: it resolved only whether the sample activities constituted qualified research, and the Section 41(c) base-period consistency rule was neither raised nor adjudicated (110 T.C. at 454 n.1, 457).
Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures
Failure to Prove Technological Uncertainty and the Evolution of the "Discovery" Standard

A primary driver of disqualification across seven of Norwest's eight sample projects was the taxpayer's inability to demonstrate that its software engineers were resolving fundamental technological uncertainty rather than executing complex but routine software engineering. In construing IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(i)—which requires that research be undertaken "for the purpose of discovering information which is technological in nature"—Judge Jacobs adopted a highly restrictive interpretation known in federal tax jurisprudence as the historical "discovery test". The Tax Court held that the statutory term "discovering" demands that the taxpayer obtain knowledge that expands or refines the existing principles of computer science—information that is "new to the world" and goes beyond the current state of knowledge among skilled professionals in the field, rather than information that is merely "new to the taxpayer" (110 T.C. at 492–494). This narrow construction was echoed later that year by the Seventh Circuit in United Stationers, Inc. v. United States, 163 F.3d 440, 444 (7th Cir. 1998), and subsequently in Eustace v. Commissioner, 312 F.3d 905 (7th Cir. 2002).

Under this stringent standard, seven of Norwest's projects failed because the Court found that they involved nothing more than "cookbook" approaches to software development and the skilled practice of computer programmers, in which the ability to accomplish the task was known at the outset through known methodologies, so that no information expanding or refining the principles of computer science was discovered (110 T.C. at 522–523). In the Success project, for example, Norwest designed an in-house equipment leasing system to replace its legacy Infolease software. Although building the replacement system required substantial coding effort and business logic mapping, the record was specifically lacking with respect to technical risk: the only activity that may have involved technical risk was developing Success on the TPF platform, the project manager testified that he never encountered insurmountable issues, and the major risks related to tight time constraints—a business risk, not a technical risk (110 T.C. at 524–525). Similarly, in the Money Transfer project, Norwest modified its vendor-supplied MoneyNet wire transfer system to address the Federal Reserve's 5 p.m. rule and daylight overdraft rule, consolidate branch wire transfers, and accommodate rapidly growing transaction volumes (110 T.C. at 475–478). The Court found that Norwest had not demonstrated any technical risks or a process of experimentation: there was no evidence of uncertainty about the ability to complete the project, no alternative designs or hypotheses were evaluated, and the work merely required good coding and eliminating bugs through testing (110 T.C. at 526).

Conversely, the Strategic Banking System (SBS) Customer Module passed the Court's scrutiny because, at the time, it represented a concerted effort at advancing the state of technology in the field of computer science, pushing existing technology to new heights (110 T.C. at 518). Begun by EDS and Bank One on August 18, 1986, and joined by Norwest under agreements executed on December 16, 1986, the SBS project sought to replace separately maintained, account-based systems with an integrated banking system in which all information centered on the customer, linking a customer module with deposit and loan (credit) modules (110 T.C. at 463–464). At the outset, the participants raised specific technical concerns—including whether the DB2 relational database could handle the projected data volume, the user architecture, and the use of the PACBASE tool—and the former president of Norwest Technical Services estimated a 50-percent chance of failure; although some integrated systems existed, none could handle the volume of data in the SBS system or was customer based (110 T.C. at 513–515). By creating a customer-based system that could integrate with other banking systems and handle large volumes of data—the Court noting that qualified research encompasses not only new technology but also the use of existing technology in new and dynamic ways—the SBS Customer Module satisfied even the Court's demanding discovery threshold (110 T.C. at 515).

From a doctrinal perspective, practitioners must distinguish between Norwest's enduring factual inquiry into technological uncertainty and its superseded "new to the world" linguistic formulation. Following intense industry criticism—and after final regulations issued in January 2001 (T.D. 8930) that retained a discovery test were suspended for review (Notice 2001-19)—the Treasury Department eliminated the discovery test in proposed regulations issued in December 2001 and then in final regulations issued in late 2003 (T.D. 9104; Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)), formally abrogating the "new to the world" discovery requirement. Modern judicial precedent, notably United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009), confirms that under current Treasury regulations, research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving a business component, or the appropriate design of that business component, based on information available to the taxpayer; Tax & Accounting Software Corp. v. United States, 301 F.3d 1254 (10th Cir. 2002), predates those final regulations. Nevertheless, even under the modern "elimination of uncertainty" standard, Norwest's seven disqualified projects would still fail because the appropriate design and method for routine vendor package installations (General Ledger, Cyborg Payroll), legacy re-writes (Success), and minor functional enhancements (Trust TU, Trust Payment, Debit Card) were readily ascertainable by skilled software engineers at the outset of development.
Absence of a Structured Process of Experimentation and Conflation with Standard SDLC

The second fatal deficiency in Norwest's claim was its conflation of the standard Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)—specifically requirements gathering, coding, systems integration, and quality assurance debugging—with a scientific "process of experimentation" under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C). As the Tax Court articulated in Norwest (110 T.C. at 496), drawing on the 1986 conference report, a process of experimentation involves the evaluation of more than one alternative designed to achieve a result where the means of achieving that result is uncertain at the outset, which may involve developing one or more hypotheses, testing and analyzing those hypotheses (for example, through modeling or simulation), and refining or discarding them as part of a sequential design process—with the required uncertainty concerning the technical ability to develop the product rather than whether it can be developed within business or economic constraints.

In examining Norwest's seven non-qualifying projects, the Court found that the capacity to accomplish each project was already part of the skilled practice and known methodologies available to Norwest's programmers, even where the exact benefits to be derived were in doubt (110 T.C. at 522–523). While the programmers encountered numerous coding bugs, formatting incompatibilities, and data mapping errors during development, resolving those issues through iterative trial-and-error debugging did not constitute hypothesis-driven experimentation. Specifically, the Court's project-by-project findings illustrate four recurring non-qualifying software patterns that taxpayers frequently misclassify as experimental research. First, in projects involving vendor package modification—such as General Ledger (customizing approximately 25 percent of the vendor-supplied Financial Control System (FCS) code and retrofitting new vendor releases) and Cyborg Payroll (customizing and maintaining a vendor payroll system acquired in the late 1970s)—Norwest's personnel retrofitted releases, redesigned inefficient components, built interfaces, wrote custom "method code," and modified reports (110 T.C. at 474–475, 479). The Court held that the only General Ledger activity that could have involved technical risk, the shadow file system, was common at large U.S. banks and required only known methodologies, and that the Cyborg work—aimed at keeping a 1970s system running into the early 1990s—involved nothing more than the skilled practice of the information technology industry (110 T.C. at 525, 527).

Second, across General Ledger, Money Transfer, and Cyborg Payroll, Norwest claimed QREs for vendor release upgrades and retrofitting, including comparing new vendor code with Norwest's existing custom modifications to preserve required functionality (110 T.C. at 474, 478, 479). Although the Court refused to adopt the Commissioner's bright-line rule that implementing vendor releases of commercially available software can never qualify, holding that such modifications must be examined case by case (110 T.C. at 500), it found the retrofitting work in these projects to be routine skilled practice rather than qualified research. Third, Norwest relied on its extensive unit testing, integrated systems testing, and acceptance testing under its Software Development Methodology across projects like Trust Payment, Debit Card, and Money Transfer. The Court rejected this contention, holding in Money Transfer that conducting good coding and eliminating bugs through testing reflected cookbook approaches and skilled practice rather than research and experimentation, finding in Trust Payment that the technical risks encountered were limited and clearly solvable, and finding in Debit Card that the only risk was completing the project before competitors (110 T.C. at 526, 528, 530).

Fourth, even within the qualifying SBS Customer Module, the Tax Court drew temporal and functional lines around the qualifying expenses (110 T.C. at 520–521). The Court held that Norwest's installation process—including interfacing SBS with Norwest's existing deposit and credit systems—and the subsequent testing were critical to the success of SBS, part of the research process, and far from routine, so that expenses through the first deployment of the customer module to each of Norwest's banks qualified; it excluded, however, customization activities after receipt of the first SBS release that were unrelated to installation and interfacing (as relating only to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors under IRC Section 41(d)(3)(B)), and any activities performed after the first SBS release was installed at each bank, noting that Norwest had not shown that subsequent SBS releases involved qualified research. Under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(A), research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component is statutorily excluded.

Furthermore, failure to segregate routine SDLC activities from genuine experimental activities destroys a project's eligibility under the "substantially all" test of IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C). In Norwest, the Court held that "substantially all" means at least 80 percent of the activities that constitute elements of a process of experimentation, consistent with the definition of "substantially all" for qualified wages in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2) (110 T.C. at 497); the requirement was later codified in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), which measures the 80 percent on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis:
Substantially-all fraction = (research activities constituting elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose) ÷ (total research activities of the business component) ≥ 80%

When a taxpayer aggregates an entire multi-year software release—bundling routine user interface coding, data migration, vendor configuration, and post-deployment debugging together with a small kernel of algorithmic experimentation—the denominator of the "substantially all" fraction swells while the numerator remains small, causing the entire business component to fall below the 80 percent threshold unless the taxpayer properly documents and applies the "shrinking-back" rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to isolate the specific experimental subcomponent.
Failure of the Three-Part High Threshold of Innovation Test for Internal Use Software

Because all eight representative projects in Norwest involved software developed primarily for the bank's internal general and administrative operations—such as accounting, payroll, trust ledger administration, and internal transaction processing—they triggered the presumptive exclusion of IRC Section 41(d)(4)(E). To overcome this exclusion, Norwest was required to satisfy all three prongs of the High Threshold of Innovation Test derived from the 1986 Conference Report and subsequently codified in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6). As Judge Jacobs emphasized (110 T.C. at 495, 499), while the general Business Component Test of IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) requires only "some level of functional improvement, at a minimum," the extent of improvements required by Congress for internal-use software is "much greater than that required in other fields".

Seven of Norwest's projects failed to qualify, although the Court generally rested those dispositions on the absence of technological discovery, a process of experimentation, or technical risk rather than on separate findings under each heightened prong (110 T.C. at 522–530). Under the Commercial Availability Prong, the taxpayer must prove that the software cannot be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for its intended purpose without modifications that themselves satisfy the innovativeness and significant economic risk requirements. In General Ledger (FCS software), Cyborg Payroll, and Trust TU (a vendor-supplied trust system purchased in 1979 and installed in 1981), Norwest actually purchased or licensed commercially available software packages from third-party vendors and customized them (110 T.C. at 467–468, 474, 478–479). While modifying a COTS package is not per se disqualified—the Court expressly refused to adopt a bright-line rule and required case-by-case examination of such modifications (110 T.C. at 500)—the Court found Norwest's modifications in these projects to be routine skilled practice rather than research. By contrast, for projects built in-house, the record showed that Norwest built Trust Payment after determining that commercially available trust systems could not meet its needs, and the Commissioner's own expert acknowledged that no commercially available software could provide exactly the functionality Norwest needed for Success; the Court did not decide those projects on commercial availability grounds but on the absence of technical risk (110 T.C. at 480, 524–525, 528).

Under the Significant Economic Risk Prong, the taxpayer must commit substantial resources to the development and face substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that those resources would be recovered within a reasonable period (110 T.C. at 499–500). A critical legal principle established in Norwest is the Court's strict separation of technical risk from business, budget, or competitive market risk. In projects such as Debit Card, Trust Payment, and Money Transfer, the record showed that the principal risks were completing the project before competitors (Norwest entered the debit card market approximately three months ahead of its nearest competitor), maintaining competitive standing under self-imposed time constraints, and business consequences such as Federal Reserve deadlines and security concerns (110 T.C. at 482–483, 526, 528–530). The Tax Court held that these were business risks rather than technical risks, and that a "reasonable period of time" for the development of a software system relates to the reasonable time of those in the field of computer science, not to self-imposed business time constraints (110 T.C. at 526, 528, 530). Only in the SBS Customer Module—where the three participants had spent an estimated $125 million by 1993, and the combination of a customer-based design, large volume capacity, and integration of new systems into a large banking environment posed serious technical challenges that made recovery of the costs within a reasonable period substantially uncertain—did the Court find significant economic risk (110 T.C. at 516–517).

Under the Innovativeness Prong, the software must be innovative, as where it results in a reduction in cost, or improvement in speed, that is substantial and economically significant; the Court declined to quantify this standard by percentage and held that only a "high threshold of innovativeness" will satisfy it (110 T.C. at 498–499). The record showed that projects like Trust TU (reducing the monthly cost per trust account from approximately $9 to $4 or $5 and nightly batch processing from about 10 hours to about 6), Success (reducing month-end processing from three or more days to overnight), General Ledger, and Cyborg Payroll improved operational workflows and efficiency (110 T.C. at 468–469, 473–475, 479). However, the Court did not resolve those projects under the innovativeness prong; it held them non-qualifying because they involved cookbook approaches, skilled practice, and business rather than technical risk, whereas for SBS it relied on unchallenged McKinsey & Co. findings of substantial efficiency and economic benefit (110 T.C. at 516, 522–527).
Contractual, Funded Research, and Substantial Rights Deficiencies

Beyond technical qualification, Norwest illustrates the contractual issues that arise when enterprises engage third-party software vendors, systems integrators, or joint-venture partners. Under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H), qualified research excludes any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person. Furthermore, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), as applied in Norwest, amounts paid to a third party qualify as contract research expenses under IRC Section 41(b)(3) only if the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the research, the research is performed on behalf of the taxpayer—which requires that the taxpayer have a right to the research results, though not necessarily exclusive rights—and the payments are not contingent on the success of the research; related regulations (now Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)) address whether a taxpayer retains substantial rights (110 T.C. at 518–519).

In Norwest, the Tax Court made no finding that Norwest lacked substantial research rights in any vendor-related project; the only contract research dispute in the opinion concerned SBS (110 T.C. at 518–520). For vendor-supplied systems, the record instead shows that Norwest acquired the MoneyNet source code from the vendor in anticipation of needed changes, that NTS reviewed old and new Cyborg source code obtained from the vendor, and that a vendor rewrote the Micro IS application for Norwest at Norwest's suggestion (110 T.C. at 470, 476, 479). Those projects failed on technical qualification grounds, not on substantial rights or funded research grounds, and the opinion contains no findings about vendor license terms vesting ownership of modifications in the vendors or requiring additional royalties.

By contrast, in the SBS Customer Module, the Court rejected the Commissioner's argument that EDS's work did not qualify as contract research performed on Norwest's behalf, preserving Norwest's Section 41(b)(3) contract research eligibility (110 T.C. at 518–520). Under the December 16, 1986 participant license agreement, EDS retained ownership of the SBS system, but Norwest received a perpetual, nontransferable, nonexclusive, royalty-free license to use the system (later extended to permit use in providing services to nonaffiliated institutions), and the Court held that this right to use the research results without paying for that right was sufficient as a "right to the research results" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(ii) and (3)—which provides that the taxpayer need not have exclusive rights—while expressly noting that such a right may or may not constitute "substantial rights" within the meaning of the regulations (110 T.C. at 518–519). Additionally, the Court examined the payment terms and found that, although Norwest could stop making payments and terminate the agreements at development milestones, the agreements contained no success contingency and Norwest could not recover payments already made, so the requirement of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii) that payments not be contingent on the success of the research was satisfied (110 T.C. at 520).
Evidentiary Substantiation and the Section 41(c) Base-Period Consistency Rule

Finally, Norwest offers lessons on two critical procedural and computational pillars of R&D tax credit administration: project-level substantiation under IRC Section 6001 and—as a separate statutory matter not adjudicated in the opinion—the mandatory base-period consistency requirement under IRC Section 41(c).

With respect to substantiation, Norwest relied on a retrospective Coopers & Lybrand study commissioned in 1994, years after the activities occurred, and the record showed that Norwest did not maintain any formal, documented method of reporting technical risk; its Software Development Methodology project risk assessment form measured process risk rather than technical risk (110 T.C. at 456–457 & n.3, 459, 462). The amounts of the expenditures themselves were largely stipulated—the parties agreed that 90.7 percent of the sample-activity expenditures were substantiated—so the opinion did not address expenditure estimation under the Cohan doctrine (Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930)); the Fifth Circuit later held in United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009), that Cohan estimation may be considered once a taxpayer proves that qualified research actually occurred, but estimation cannot cure a failure to prove the underlying Section 41(d) qualification tests. Consistent with the taxpayer's burden of proof—tax credits being a matter of legislative grace (110 T.C. at 488 n.34)—the Court disallowed Success in part because the record was specifically lacking with respect to the technical risks involved (110 T.C. at 524); project names, software version numbers, and lump-sum IT cost centers do not independently prove what specific uncertainties an engineer addressed or what fraction of hours was devoted to hypothesis testing.

On the computational side, the IRC Section 41(c) Consistency Rule—currently at IRC § 41(c)(5)(A) for the regular credit and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(c)(2) for the Alternative Simplified Credit—was not at issue in 110 T.C. 454, which was consolidated solely on whether Norwest's activities constituted qualified research (110 T.C. at 454 n.1); the rule nonetheless operates by statute to neutralize the artificial tax benefit that asymmetric credit-year claims would otherwise generate. The Section 41 research credit is fundamentally an incremental incentive: under the regular credit method, a taxpayer receives a 20 percent credit only for credit-year QREs that exceed a "base amount," which for taxable years beginning after 1989 is generally calculated by multiplying the taxpayer's "fixed-base percentage" (for most established taxpayers, the ratio of aggregate QREs to aggregate gross receipts during the 1984–1988 base period) by the average annual gross receipts for the four preceding tax years, whereas for the earlier credit years at issue in Norwest the base amount was generally the average of the taxpayer's QREs for the three preceding taxable years. Under the modern Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) of IRC Section 41(c)(4), the credit equals 14 percent of credit-year QREs exceeding 50 percent of the average QREs for the three preceding tax years.

Because Norwest had not claimed the research credit on any of its returns for 1986 through 1991 and first asserted it through amended Tax Court petitions based on the 1994 Coopers & Lybrand study, the posture of the case illustrates how a retrospective study can raise base-period questions (110 T.C. at 456 n.3); the opinion, however, does not discuss Norwest's base-period QREs or decide whether its base period was adjusted. As a matter of statute and regulation, the consistency requirement of Section 41(c) is mandatory and non-elective: if a taxpayer expands its definition of qualified research to include a category of internal-use software expenditures in the claim year, it must determine its base-period QREs on the same basis—regardless of whether the statute of limitations for the base years is closed. Failure to apply symmetric definitions creates a purely definitional increment rather than a genuine increase in research investment, rendering asymmetric R&D credit studies structurally noncompliant.
Comparative Summary Table
Mapping of Legal Requirements, Taxpayer Failures, and Judicial Standards of Proof

The following table maps each statutory, regulatory, and judicial requirement analyzed in Norwest Corp. v. Commissioner—together with related statutory requirements that the opinion did not adjudicate—against the specific deficiencies exhibited by Norwest's disqualified claims (or, where the opinion is silent, the corresponding risk) and the governing standard of proof established by the Tax Court or by the applicable statute and regulations.

headers: Court's Standard of Proof & Modern Doctrinal Evolution

cells: 1. Section 174 / 174A Expenditure Eligibility (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), IRC § 174, IRC § 174A, Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2)

No failure: the Commissioner conceded that the expenditures associated with all eight sample activities may be treated as expenses under § 174, and the Court held that each sample activity therefore satisfied the elements for a § 174 deduction (110 T.C. at 490–491).

Taxpayer must satisfy all elements for a deduction under § 174 (110 T.C. at 491): the activity must constitute research and development in the experimental/laboratory sense (eliminating uncertainty as to capability, method, or design) and the expenditure must be of a nature eligible under § 174 (or domestic § 174A post-2024 under Pub. L. 119-21). Satisfying § 174/174A is necessary but not sufficient for § 41, because the § 41 discovery test is narrower (110 T.C. at 492–493).
2. Discovery / Technological Information Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3))

Relied on established computer science principles, known methodologies, and skilled practice ("cookbook" approaches) to build or adapt banking applications (Success, Money Transfer, Trust Payment) where the ability to develop the software was known to skilled programmers (110 T.C. at 522–528).

Historical Norwest Standard: Required discovering information that exceeds what is known in the field—not merely new to the taxpayer—by expanding or refining principles of computer science (110 T.C. at 493–494). Modern Regulatory Standard: Requires proving via objective technical evidence that information available to the taxpayer at project outset did not establish the capability, method, or appropriate design of the business component (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3), T.D. 9104).
3. Business Component & Shrink-Back Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), IRC § 41(d)(2), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2))

Not a basis for disallowance in Norwest: the experts conceded the activities provided new or improved business functions to Norwest, and the Court applied the shrinking-back test case by case, examining the SBS activities in toto because they were interdependent (110 T.C. at 498, 509, 512, 516).

Taxpayer must identify the discrete product, process, or software business component and demonstrate an intent to achieve at least "some level of functional improvement" (110 T.C. at 495). If the overall system fails the requirements, the shrinking-back test is applied to the most significant subset of elements that satisfies them, determined case by case (110 T.C. at 497–498).
4. Process of Experimentation & "Substantially All" Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), IRC § 41(d)(3), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6))

Conflated standard SDLC activities—requirements definition, writing code using known methods, vendor package integration, and routine QA/debugging (Trust TU, Debit Card, Cyborg Payroll)—with scientific experimentation.

Taxpayer must prove that at least 80% of the activities (Norwest, 110 T.C. at 497; later regulations measure on a cost or other consistently applied basis) constitute elements of a process evaluating more than one alternative to resolve technical uncertainty for a qualified purpose (function, performance, reliability, quality). Routine trial-and-error debugging does not qualify.
5. IUS Prong 1: High Threshold of Innovativeness (IRC § 41(d)(4)(E), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6))

Claimed credits for back-office automation, legacy system replacements (Success), and regulatory updates (Money Transfer) that improved efficiency; the Court disallowed these on discovery, experimentation, and technical-risk grounds rather than by separate innovativeness findings (110 T.C. at 524–526).

For internal-use software, the extent of required improvement is "much greater than that required in other fields" (110 T.C. at 499). Software must result in a reduction in cost, or improvement in speed, that is substantial and economically significant; the Court refused to quantify this by percentage and required a "high threshold of innovativeness" (110 T.C. at 498–499).
6. IUS Prong 2: Significant Economic Risk (IRC § 41(d)(4)(E), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6))

Equated commercial, competitive, and scheduling risks (e.g., being first in its market with a debit card product, self-imposed deadlines, or management-driven delays) with technical risk (110 T.C. at 528–530).

Taxpayer must prove it committed substantial resources to development and faced substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that those resources would be recovered within a reasonable period; a "reasonable period" is measured by those in the field of computer science, not by self-imposed business time constraints (110 T.C. at 499–500, 528).
7. IUS Prong 3: Commercial Availability (IRC § 41(d)(4)(E), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6))

Purchased or licensed existing vendor software (General Ledger, Cyborg Payroll, Trust TU) and performed routine customization; for the in-house Success and Trust Payment systems, the record suggested no commercial product met Norwest's exact needs, and the Court decided those projects on other grounds (110 T.C. at 480, 524, 528).

Software must not be commercially available for use without modifications that satisfy the innovativeness and significant economic risk tests; the Court refused a bright-line rule that vendor releases can never qualify and examines modifications case by case (110 T.C. at 500). A documented evaluation of commercial alternatives—such as Norwest's pre-SBS review and rejection of the Hogan product—strengthens the record (110 T.C. at 463–464, 517–518).
8. Substantial Rights & Contract Research Eligibility (IRC § 41(b)(3), IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), § 1.41-4A(d))

No such failure was found: the only contract research dispute concerned SBS, where the Court held that Norwest had a right to EDS's research results and that its payments were not contingent on success (110 T.C. at 518–520).

The contractor must perform the research on behalf of the taxpayer (the taxpayer must have a right to the research results, which need not be exclusive), and payments must not be contingent on the success of the research (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3)). A perpetual, royalty-free license to use the results, as in SBS, was sufficient as a right to the research results, although the Court left open whether it constitutes "substantial rights" (110 T.C. at 519).
9. Base-Period Consistency Mandate (IRC § 41(c)(5)(A) / former § 41(c)(6), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(d), § 1.41-9(c)(2))

Not adjudicated: the opinion resolved only whether the sample activities were qualified research; Norwest had not claimed the credit on its original 1986–1991 returns and asserted it through amended petitions (110 T.C. at 454 n.1, 456 n.3).

Mandatory symmetric determination (by statute and regulation, not by holding of this opinion): base-period QREs (both under the Regular Credit fixed-base percentage and the 3-year ASC lookback) must be defined and quantified using the exact same inclusion criteria applied to the claim year.
10. Recordkeeping & Expenditure Substantiation (IRC § 6001, Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d))

Expenditure amounts were largely stipulated (90.7% substantiated); however, Norwest maintained no formal, documented method of reporting technical risk, and the record for Success was specifically lacking on technical risk (110 T.C. at 457, 462, 524).

Taxpayer bears the burden of proving entitlement to the credit, which is a matter of legislative grace (110 T.C. at 488 n.34). Usable records should establish a reliable nexus between specific employees/contractors, their qualified services (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)), and the specific qualifying business component. Cohan estimation, not addressed in Norwest, applies under § 41(b) only after § 41(d) qualification is proven (McFerrin).

body.text: Project-by-Project Breakdown of the Eight Representative Software Activities in Norwest

To illustrate how the Tax Court applied the seven-part test and contractual rules to concrete banking technology facts, the following table summarizes the judicial outcome for each of the eight stipulated test projects.

cells: 1. Strategic Banking System (SBS) – Customer Module
Integrated, customer-centric banking information system (110 T.C. at 463).

Joint effort with EDS and Bank One (Norwest joining in December 1986) to replace separately maintained account-based systems with an integrated system centered on the customer, interfaced with deposit and loan modules and able to handle large data volumes; Norwest served as the test bed for roughly three years of testing and redesign (110 T.C. at 463–467).

None for development through first deployment at each Norwest bank. However, customization after receipt of the first SBS release unrelated to installation and interfacing was excluded under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) (style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors), activities after the first release was installed at each bank were excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A), and the deposit and credit modules did not qualify for lack of evidence (110 T.C. at 514–515, 521).

QUALIFIED (In Part): Customer module development through first deployment at each bank qualified (satisfied all 7 tests; perpetual royalty-free license from EDS established a right to the research results) (110 T.C. at 518–521). Later customization disallowed.
2. Trust TU
Trust account administration and fiduciary reporting.

Hundreds of projects on a vendor-supplied trust system (purchased in 1979, installed in 1981), including batch-processing concurrency work, a Fasttax tax-reporting interface, and Micro IS portfolio system changes (110 T.C. at 467–470).

Failed Discovery and Process of Experimentation (cookbook approaches and skilled practice; nothing new accomplished; capacity already achieved elsewhere); risks were solely business risks, not technical risks (110 T.C. at 522–523). No findings on substantial rights.
DISQUALIFIED: 0% QREs allowed.
3. Success
Equipment leasing operations and lease accounting.
In-house design and coding of an equipment leasing platform to replace the existing Infolease system.

Record specifically lacking on technical risk; the only possible technical risk (developing on the TPF platform) was vaguely supported and a small part of the project; major risks were time constraints (business risk); project did not venture into uncharted territory (110 T.C. at 524–525).
DISQUALIFIED: 0% QREs allowed.
4. General Ledger
Corporate accounting, financial consolidations, and reporting.

Customization of approximately 25% of the vendor-supplied FCS code, retrofitting of new vendor releases, consolidation redesign and automation, a "shadow file" system, and batch scheduling (110 T.C. at 473–475).

The only activity possibly involving technical risk—the shadow file system—was common at large U.S. banks and required only known methodologies; routine development that did not expand or refine computer science principles or involve technical risk (110 T.C. at 525). No findings on substantial rights.
DISQUALIFIED: 0% QREs allowed.
5. Money Transfer
Electronic funds transfer (wire transfers) and settlement.

Modifications to the vendor-supplied MoneyNet system for the Federal Reserve 5 p.m. rule (contingency site) and daylight overdraft rule, a distributed wire consolidation project, and retrofitting of vendor releases (110 T.C. at 475–478).

No demonstration of technical risk or a process of experimentation; no uncertainty about ability to complete; no alternative designs or hypotheses; obvious business risks only; good coding and bug elimination through testing (110 T.C. at 526).
DISQUALIFIED: 0% QREs allowed.
6. Cyborg Payroll
Employee payroll administration and tax withholding.

Customization and maintenance of a vendor payroll system acquired in the late 1970s (custom "method code," report changes, new releases), and conversion of acquired banks' payroll data (110 T.C. at 478–480).

Goal was to keep an outdated 1970s system running, not to advance computer science principles; efforts involved nothing more than the skilled practice of the information technology industry (110 T.C. at 526–527). No findings on substantial rights.
DISQUALIFIED: 0% QREs allowed.
7. Trust Payment
Automated pension trust disbursements, check processing, and tax reporting (110 T.C. at 480).

In-house development (1987) on IBM's DB2 relational database, resolving slow processing, negative-amount checks, and crashes under concurrent access, followed by a two-year performance review (110 T.C. at 480–481).

Technical risks arose but were limited and clearly solvable; no substantial uncertainty that the investment could be recovered within a reasonable period, which is not measured by self-imposed business time constraints (110 T.C. at 528).
DISQUALIFIED: 0% QREs allowed.
8. Debit Card
Retail debit card transaction routing and processing.

Building the debit card system on the Base 24 ATM operating system and connecting the Visanet module (Norwest being the first bank to do so), redesigning code to fix settlement communication failures with Visa (110 T.C. at 482–483).

Only risk was completing and deploying the product before competitors; no technical risks identified; debit cards were fairly common; alternatives considered (credit card processor vs. direct access) related entirely to business concerns (110 T.C. at 529–530).
DISQUALIFIED: 0% QREs allowed.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial principles of Norwest Corp. v. Commissioner into actionable tax governance, the following two industry case studies examine realistic enterprise projects that directly encounter the legal, technical, contractual, and computational pitfalls identified by the Tax Court. Each case study provides a rigorous, step-by-step remedial blueprint demonstrating how the taxpayer can restructure its project architecture, documentation, contracts, and accounting systems to withstand IRS Large Business and International (LB&I) examination and satisfy IRC Section 41.
Case Study 1: Enterprise Core Banking & Real-Time Liquidity Ledger Modernization (FinTech / Commercial Banking)
Fact Pattern and Initial Norwest Vulnerability Profile

Apex National Bancorp ("Apex"), a U.S. regional bank holding company, initiates a three-year, $18 million technology initiative titled "Project Horizon" to modernize its corporate treasury, wire transfer, and general ledger reconciliation infrastructure. To execute Project Horizon, Apex licenses a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) cloud-native core accounting package from a third-party vendor ("FinCore Corp.") and engages an external systems integrator ("GlobalSys LLC") under a Master Services Agreement (MSA) to help customize the platform, migrate legacy mainframe accounts, build a real-time Federal Reserve FedNow and ISO 20022 instant wire settlement engine, and develop a proprietary, low-latency algorithmic liquidity-sweeping engine that dynamically reallocates intraday collateral across thousands of corporate sub-accounts in under 15 milliseconds.

In its un-remediated state, Apex's tax department plans to claim 85 percent of the entire $18 million Project Horizon budget as QREs under IRC Section 41—directly mirroring the errors that defeated Norwest's General Ledger, Money Transfer, and Cyborg Payroll claims and the excluded post-deployment SBS customization. First, Apex suffers from severe business component over-aggregation by treating "Project Horizon" as a single monolithic business component, commingling $12 million of routine FinCore COTS configuration, user interface customization, ISO 20022 message formatting, and legacy data migration with $6 million of genuine algorithmic research on the intraday liquidity-sweeping engine. Because the non-experimental COTS configuration and data migration represent 67 percent of total project costs, the overall project fails the 80 percent "substantially all" Process of Experimentation threshold under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6).

Second, because the general ledger and internal liquidity management modules serve Apex's internal general and administrative financial management functions, the IRS classifies the entire project as Internal Use Software under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6). Apex possesses no contemporaneous market gap study proving why FinCore's off-the-shelf modules could not be used without fundamental modification, and its project charter cites "regulatory compliance with Federal Reserve instant payment standards and beating competing regional banks to market" as the primary project risks—falling squarely into the Money Transfer and Debit Card commercial and regulatory risk trap. Third, under the standard FinCore license agreement, any custom code or modifications touching the FinCore API automatically vest in FinCore Corp., leaving Apex with only a non-exclusive, terminable term license subject to annual maintenance fee increases—a materially weaker position than the perpetual, royalty-free license that the Court found sufficient as a right to the research results in SBS (110 T.C. at 518–519). Simultaneously, the GlobalSys LLC systems integration contract is structured as a fixed-price turnkey deliverable where GlobalSys warrants successful performance and is paid only upon user acceptance sign-off, shifting the financial risk of failure onto GlobalSys and disqualifying Apex's contract research claim under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e). Fourth, Apex historically claimed zero internal-use software QREs in its three prior tax years (2023–2025) under the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC), and plans to include Project Horizon in 2026 without adjusting its 2023–2025 base period, violating IRC Section 41(c).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Project Governance, Business Component Segregation, and Dual-Function Software Classification

To prevent routine COTS installation and data migration from contaminating the experimental core, Apex's tax advisor and Chief Technology Officer (CTO) must restructure Project Horizon's work breakdown structure (WBS) prior to or at the inception of development, establishing discrete business components under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). Apex formally carves out three non-qualifying sub-projects into separate accounting cost centers (Cost Centers 101 through 103): FinCore COTS base installation and chart-of-accounts parameter configuration; legacy mainframe data cleansing and migration; and standard ISO 20022 / FedNow message schema mapping and regulatory reporting. While domestic software development labor in these cost centers may be deductible under newly enacted IRC Section 174A (per Public Law 119-21), they are explicitly excluded from the Section 41 QRE pool.

Next, invoking the shrinking-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), Apex establishes two isolated, research-specific business components with dedicated Jira epics and general ledger project codes. Business Component A (Cost Center 201) is defined as the Distributed Intraday Liquidity-Sweeping Engine, an autonomous in-memory state machine classified as Internal Use Software that is designed to resolve distributed database lock-contention across 500,000 concurrent corporate sub-accounts. Business Component B (Cost Center 202) is defined as the Corporate Client Real-Time Treasury Portal & Automated Sweep Execution API. Under modern Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv), software developed both for internal G&A functions and to enable third-party customers to initiate transactions or review account data online is classified as Dual-Function Software. By documenting at the outset of development that corporate banking clients will directly interact with Cost Center 202 to execute automated liquidity sweeps and view real-time collateral positions, Apex can isolate the specific third-party-facing subset—which is completely exempt from the IUS High Threshold of Innovation test—or apply the Dual-Function 25 Percent Safe Harbor under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C), allowing 25 percent of the remaining dual-function subset's QREs to be included provided at least 10 percent of the software's use is estimated to be by third parties.

Finally, following the Norwest holding on the SBS Customer Module, Apex institutes a formal governance cutoff gate ("Production Readiness Gate 4"). Once the Distributed Intraday Liquidity-Sweeping Engine passes initial live environmental pilot validation and resolves its concurrency and latency uncertainties, Cost Center 201 is locked to further QRE charges. Any subsequent rollout to additional regional bank branches or customer-specific user interface tailoring is routed to a post-production maintenance code excluded under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(A).
Step 2: Technical Documentation of Commercial Unavailability and High Threshold of Innovation

For Business Component A (Cost Center 201), which remains classified as Internal Use Software, Apex builds a contemporaneous technical record satisfying all three prongs of the Norwest and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii) High Threshold of Innovation test. To prove Commercial Unavailability (IUS Prong 3) prior to writing code for Cost Center 201, Apex's architecture review board compiles a Formal COTS Technical Gap and Benchmark Analysis. The document records empirical benchmark tests run on FinCore's native liquidity module and two competing commercial treasury packages, proving that existing commercial software relies on disk-bound relational ACID transactions that cap throughput at 800 transactions per second (TPS) with 450ms latency—rendering them technologically incapable of meeting Apex's architectural requirement of 25,000 TPS at sub-15ms latency without fundamental re-engineering of the underlying concurrency control protocol.

To prove the High Threshold of Innovativeness (IUS Prong 1), the Project Charter for Cost Center 201 eliminates all references to clerical labor savings or regulatory compliance deadlines, instead documenting quantifiable computer science innovation metrics: achieving a 30-fold improvement in transaction throughput (from 800 TPS to 25,000 TPS) and a 96 percent reduction in settlement latency (from 450ms to under 15ms) by inventing a novel optimistic lock-free Conflict-Free Replicated Data Type (CRDT) ledger reconciliation algorithm. To prove Significant Economic Risk Tied Strictly to Technical Uncertainty (IUS Prong 2), Apex's Capital Allocation Committee executes a contemporaneous Technical Risk and Resource Commitment Memorandum authorizing $4.2 million in dedicated engineering capital for Cost Center 201. Rather than citing competitor market share or Federal Reserve regulatory penalties—which Norwest treated as business rather than technical risks in Money Transfer and Debit Card—the memorandum explicitly documents the computer science uncertainty: it is unknown whether an eventually consistent CRDT data structure can be mathematically reconciled with strict double-entry banking atomic settlement guarantees without causing phantom overdrafts or memory heap exhaustion under peak intraday market volatility. If the lock-free architecture fails to maintain strict serializability under stress testing, the entire $4.2 million codebase cannot be salvaged or repurposed and must be written off.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring for Substantial Rights and Financial Risk

To avoid the type of contract research challenge the Commissioner raised against SBS in Norwest and ensure that payments to GlobalSys LLC qualify as 65 percent contract research expenses under IRC Section 41(b)(3), Apex's tax counsel amends the vendor and contractor agreements before the research is performed, as mandated by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2). First, to decouple intellectual property ownership from the COTS vendor, Apex executes an Intellectual Property Addendum with FinCore Corp. stipulating that the Distributed Intraday Liquidity-Sweeping Engine (Cost Center 201) is developed as an independent, standalone middleware microservice that communicates with FinCore solely via external message queues. Under the addendum, 100 percent of the source code, algorithms, patents, and trade secrets developed in Cost Center 201 vest exclusively in Apex National Bancorp—or, to the extent FinCore assists, Apex receives a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free worldwide license to use, modify, reproduce, and commercially exploit the code without paying any additional licensing or maintenance fees, going beyond the SBS arrangement in Norwest (a perpetual, nontransferable, nonexclusive, royalty-free license to use, with EDS retaining ownership), which the Court found sufficient as a right to the research results (110 T.C. at 518–519).

Second, Apex restructures the systems integrator contract with GlobalSys LLC by replacing the turnkey fixed-price Statement of Work (SOW) for Cost Center 201 with a dedicated Time-and-Materials (T&M) Experimental Engineering Statement of Work (SOW #201-R&D). SOW #201-R&D explicitly states that GlobalSys engineers are performing computer science research and experimentation on behalf of Apex to resolve the documented CRDT concurrency uncertainties, that Apex is obligated to pay GlobalSys for hours incurred on a bi-weekly T&M basis regardless of whether the experimental architecture succeeds or fails (placing the financial risk of technical failure squarely on Apex under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii)), and that all intellectual property and experimental work product created by GlobalSys under SOW #201-R&D is "work made for hire" owned exclusively by Apex.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Base-Period Consistency Compliance

To satisfy IRC Section 6001 substantiation and the statutory consistency mandate of IRC Section 41(c), Apex embeds scientific method tracking directly into its software engineering workflow. Within Jira and GitHub, every engineering sprint in Cost Center 201 is linked to a structured Experimental Protocol Ticket containing four mandatory fields: Specific Technical Uncertainty (e.g., whether Raft consensus versus a hybrid logical clock CRDT can maintain sub-15ms p99 latency above 20,000 TPS); Competing Technical Hypotheses (Hypothesis A: Sharded Raft cluster; Hypothesis B: Vector-clock CRDT with deterministic merge); Experimental Testing Procedure (automated chaos-engineering load simulation injecting 50,000 synthetic wire bursts); and Empirical Test Results and Architectural Iteration (documenting that Raft failed at 11,200 TPS with 85ms tail latency due to leader election bottlenecks, whereas the CRDT prototype achieved 26,400 TPS at 11.4ms latency but required a custom anti-entropy gossip protocol to resolve split-brain states).

Simultaneously, Apex configures its time-tracking software so that software engineers and direct supervisors (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)) log hours daily against specific experimental Jira tickets within Cost Center 201, ensuring that over 92 percent of Cost Center 201 hours are directly tied to hypothesis formulation, prototype coding, and experimental load simulation—comfortably exceeding the 80 percent "substantially all" threshold. Finally, before filing Form 6765 for tax year 2026, Apex's tax advisor conducts a Three-Year Historical Base-Period Lookback Study (2023–2025) applying the exact same seven-part IUS qualification criteria used in 2026. By identifying and substantiating qualifying IUS and dual-function software QREs incurred during 2023, 2024, and 2025 and incorporating them into the 3-year ASC base average, Apex fully satisfies the Section 41(c) consistency mandate and avoids the 6 percent reduced ASC rate that applies when a taxpayer has no QREs in any one of the three preceding tax years (IRC § 41(c)(4)(B)).
Case Study 2: Legacy Leasing & Automated Asset Administration Platform Re-Architecture (Equipment Finance & Fiduciary Services)
Fact Pattern and Initial Norwest Vulnerability Profile

Meridian Financial Group ("Meridian"), a large equipment leasing and institutional trust custodian, launches a $12 million internal software initiative ("Project Vanguard") to replace its 25-year-old COBOL mainframe equipment leasing and trust disbursement systems—a factual scenario directly analogous to Norwest's disqualified Success (replacing Infolease), Trust TU, and Trust Payment projects. Meridian's internal IT department of 65 software developers is tasked with rewriting the legacy COBOL business rules into a modern Java and Kubernetes microservices architecture, consolidating three separate regional trust payment databases into a single PostgreSQL schema, building a modern React web dashboard for internal lease administrators, and integrating a newly developed Automated Predictive Residual-Value & Dynamic Securitizations Engine that uses stochastic Monte Carlo simulations and graph-neural-network (GNN) credit-contagion algorithms to re-price millions of equipment leases and trust asset pools in real time without crashing the production database.

In its un-remediated posture, Meridian faces total disallowance under Norwest for three primary reasons. First, Meridian falls directly into the "legacy re-write and porting" disqualification exemplified by the Success project in Norwest. Meridian's tax director plans to claim the wages of all 65 developers across the entire $12 million legacy migration, arguing that translating undocumented 25-year-old COBOL code into Java microservices required "extensive trial and error" and "discovering how the old system worked". Under Norwest, United Stationers, and the IRS Audit Guidelines for Software, reverse-engineering legacy code, porting existing functionality to a modern programming language, database consolidation, and graphical user interface (GUI) updates fail both the Technological Uncertainty test and the Process of Experimentation test.

Second, Meridian lacks contemporaneous documentation and relies on arbitrary percentage estimates. Because the company does not use project time-tracking, department managers provide retrospective interview estimates claiming that "roughly 70 percent to 80 percent of every developer's time was spent solving hard technical problems and testing code". Because the taxpayer bears the burden of proof under Norwest—where the Court disallowed Success in part because the record was specifically lacking on technical risk—unsupported percentage estimates coupled with standard quality assurance debugging records expose the claim to complete disallowance, because a court has no principled basis to separate experimental work from routine software development (110 T.C. at 488 n.34, 524). Third, Meridian fails to differentiate operational efficiency from IUS innovativeness: its internal business case justifies Project Vanguard on the grounds that retiring the mainframe will save $3 million annually in IBM mainframe licensing fees and reduce manual lease processing time by 40 percent. Under the "high threshold of innovativeness" adopted in Norwest (110 T.C. at 499), cost savings from retiring legacy hardware and routine workflow automation are unlikely to satisfy the IUS High Threshold of Innovation, particularly where the underlying work is cookbook software development.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Pre-Development Uncertainty Gateways and Granular Subcomponent Isolation

To rescue the genuinely innovative technological core of Project Vanguard from being disqualified by the broader legacy re-write, Meridian applies the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) Shrinking-Back Rule at the architectural governance level before claiming any QREs. Meridian's R&D Tax Governance Committee establishes a hard accounting boundary separating the legacy COBOL-to-Java re-write (50 developers, $9.2 million) from the experimental computational engineering team (15 specialized distributed-systems and quantitative engineers, $2.8 million). The committee documents that translating legacy lease accounting formulas into Java, consolidating PostgreSQL tables, and building the React GUI involve known software engineering methodologies and are excluded from the Section 41 claim, though tracked separately as domestic software development expenditures under IRC Section 174A.

Meridian then defines two narrow, mathematically rigorous software business components staffed exclusively by the 15-person advanced engineering group. Business Component 1 (BC-1) is designated as the Vectorized GPU-Accelerated Monte Carlo Lease Securitizations Engine, a custom C++ and CUDA computational kernel embedded within the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) via Project Panama (Foreign Function & Memory API) designed to execute 100 million correlated stochastic path simulations across 2 million equipment leases in under 3 seconds. Business Component 2 (BC-2) is designated as the Zero-Copy Streaming Graph-Contagion Trust Risk Engine, a custom off-heap memory management and graph-traversal algorithm designed to detect cross-counterparty default contagion across multi-tiered fiduciary trust structures in real time without triggering JVM Stop-The-World garbage collection pauses.
Step 2: Technical Documentation of Computer Science Uncertainty and IUS High Threshold of Innovation

To satisfy Norwest's stringent standards for Internal Use Software on BC-1 and BC-2, Meridian's Principal Systems Architect compiles a Contemporaneous Pre-Development Technical Feasibility & Commercial Availability Dossier prior to sprint execution. To document Commercial Unavailability (IUS Prong 3), the dossier preserves formal Request for Proposal (RFP) responses and technical evaluations of three leading commercial equipment leasing and risk analytics suites, proving that no commercial software on the market supports real-time, off-heap JVM-to-GPU zero-copy stochastic simulation across million-node equipment lease portfolios. Because commercial packages rely on overnight batch processing taking 6 to 8 hours, real-time intraday securitization pricing is impossible without custom algorithmic development.

To establish Fundamental Computer Science Uncertainty and Significant Economic Risk (IUS Prong 2), the dossier details why skilled computer scientists cannot establish the capability, method, or appropriate design of BC-1 and BC-2 at the outset under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3). For BC-1, transferring multi-gigabyte lease state matrices between JVM heap memory and GPU VRAM over PCIe buses introduces serialization bottlenecks that theoretically negate the GPU's parallel compute speed; furthermore, floating-point non-associativity in parallel GPU thread warps causes numerical drift that violates fiduciary accounting precision requirements. For BC-2, standard JVM garbage collectors (G1GC, ZGC) suffer catastrophic latency spikes when mutating cyclic graph pointers at 100,000 updates per second. Meridian's Board of Directors formally ring-fences the $2.8 million budget for BC-1 and BC-2 as High-Risk Experimental R&D Capital, documenting that if the engineering team cannot resolve the PCIe memory-transfer bottleneck and floating-point determinism problem, the $2.8 million investment in BC-1 and BC-2 will be completely unrecoverable because the institution will be forced to fall back to conventional overnight batch processing. To quantify the High Threshold of Innovativeness (IUS Prong 1), rather than citing IBM mainframe licensing savings, the dossier establishes objective computer science performance targets: reducing portfolio simulation execution time from 7.5 hours (27,000 seconds) to under 3.0 seconds—a 9,000-fold speed improvement—while maintaining IEEE 754 bit-wise reproducibility across heterogeneous GPU clusters.
Step 3: Inter-Company Contractual Governance and Rights Preservation

Because Meridian operates as a parent holding company with multiple operating leasing and trust subsidiaries—mirroring the corporate structure of Norwest Corporation and Subsidiaries—it must align its inter-company and external contracts with IRC Section 41(f)(1) and Section 41(d)(4)(H). Under IRC Section 41(f)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-6, all members of a controlled group of corporations (more than 50 percent common ownership) are treated as a single taxpayer for purposes of computing the research credit. However, to avoid any third-party "funded research" or substantial rights challenge under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) when external cloud GPU labs or university mathematics consultants are retained, Meridian ensures that all external consulting contracts are executed prior to performance, explicitly vest 100 percent of intellectual property rights in Meridian without ongoing royalty obligations, contain no performance guarantees or refund clauses by the contractors, and obligate Meridian to pay for all research hours incurred regardless of technical outcome.
Step 4: Scientific Process of Experimentation Tracking and the 80% "Substantially All" Fraction

To eliminate the evidentiary failures that doomed Norwest's seven non-qualifying projects and withstood scrutiny only in SBS, Meridian restructures its software testing pipeline into two legally distinct tracks. The first track—Experimental Hypothesis Testing (Qualifying)—is conducted exclusively by the 15-person advanced engineering team inside a dedicated Architecture Benchmark Lab. Every code commit in BC-1 and BC-2 is tied to an automated Hypothesis Evaluation Log documenting alternative algorithmic designs tested (such as evaluating Kahan compensated summation versus double-double precision arithmetic on CUDA cores, and testing custom slab-allocated off-heap arena memory versus Rust JNI native bindings for graph traversal), complete with flame graphs, memory telemetry, and latency histograms proving why specific hypotheses failed and how the architecture evolved. The second track—Functional QA, Regression, and User Acceptance Testing (Non-Qualifying)—begins only after the BC-1 and BC-2 engines achieve their sub-3.0-second latency and numerical accuracy targets in the lab; at that point, integration into the broader Java leasing platform and routine bug fixing are transferred to the general QA team and charged to the non-qualifying SDLC cost center.

To substantiate the "substantially all" (≥ 80%) fraction and establish a bulletproof wage nexus under IRC Section 6001, Meridian implements contemporaneous bi-weekly timecards requiring the 15 engineers in BC-1 and BC-2 to allocate their hours across four specific activity codes: Hypothesis Formulation and Algorithmic Design (Code 1); Experimental Prototype Coding (Code 2); Empirical Benchmark Simulation and Failure Analysis (Code 3); and Routine Administration and Maintenance (Code 4). Contemporaneous payroll records demonstrate that 89.4 percent of total labor costs in BC-1 and 91.2 percent of total labor costs in BC-2 were spent on Activity Codes 1, 2, and 3. Because both business components exceed the 80 percent "substantially all" threshold under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), 100 percent of the qualified wages—along with dedicated cloud GPU compute rental costs used directly in running experimental simulations to the extent eligible under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4)—are substantiated for the credit, while the non-qualifying $9.2 million COBOL re-write is cleanly excluded from the Form 6765 claim.
Comparative Summary of Remediation Outcomes Across Case Studies

The table below synthesizes how the structural interventions in Case Study 1 and Case Study 2 directly resolve the legal and evidentiary failures identified in Norwest Corp. v. Commissioner, together with related statutory requirements that the opinion did not adjudicate.

cells: Over-Broad Business Component & "Substantially All" Dilution (SBS Post-Deployment & General Projects)
Bundled $12M+ of routine COTS configuration, UI coding, and COBOL porting with core algorithmic R&D, dropping experimental activities below 80%.
Applied Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) shrink-back rule at project inception to isolate experimental engines into dedicated WBS cost centers; cut off QREs at initial production readiness gate.
Numerator/denominator of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) fraction exceeds 89%–92% on isolated subcomponents, satisfying IRC § 41(d)(1)(C).
IUS Commercial Availability & COTS Customization Trap (risk illustrated by General Ledger, Cyborg Payroll, Trust TU, Success)
Licensed COTS packages or built in-house replacements without proving why commercial software could not meet technical requirements.
Executed pre-development RFP & empirical benchmark gap studies proving COTS software capped out at 800 TPS / 7.5-hour batch runs and could not operate without fundamental algorithmic invention.
Satisfies Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C) Commercial Unavailability prong; also isolates Dual-Function software under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv).
Conflating Market/Regulatory Risk with Technical Risk (Money Transfer, Debit Card)
Cited Federal Reserve compliance deadlines, competitor speed-to-market, and mainframe license cost savings as project risks.
Documented capital-at-risk memos tying economic risk strictly to computer science uncertainties (CRDT serializability vs. sub-15ms latency; PCIe GPU bottleneck and IEEE 754 drift).
Satisfies Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(B) Significant Economic Risk and (A) High Threshold of Innovativeness (30-fold to 9,000-fold speed gains).
Conflating Standard SDLC & Debugging with Experimentation (All 7 Failed Projects)
Treated requirements gathering, COBOL-to-Java translation, database migration, and QA bug-fixing as a process of experimentation.
Segregated functional QA from Architecture Benchmark Lab; instituted mandatory Jira Experimental Protocol Tickets tracking hypotheses, alternatives, chaos/load tests, and telemetry.
Establishes a systematic, scientific process of experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5).
Contract Research Rights in Vendor/Contractor Code (SBS EDS Contract)
Allowed COTS vendor to retain IP ownership of custom modifications; used turnkey fixed-price integrator contract where vendor bore risk.
Executed pre-research IP addendum vesting exclusive ownership / perpetual royalty-free license in taxpayer; converted integrator SOW to T&M where taxpayer bears financial risk of failure.
Preserves "substantial rights" and avoids funded research exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), § 41(b)(3), and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e).
Asymmetric Base Period & Retrospective Estimation (IRC § 41(c) Consistency & § 6001 — statutory requirements not adjudicated in Norwest)
Claimed expansive IUS QREs in credit year with $0 IUS QREs in base period; relied on retrospective manager percentage guesses.
Conducted symmetric 3-year ASC base-period lookback study applying identical IUS criteria; implemented contemporaneous ticket-level time tracking.
Satisfies IRC § 41(c)(5)(A) / Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(c)(2) consistency rule and IRC § 6001 / Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) substantiation.
